sentences.text:
The
acc
used Ram Singh is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Kwality Sweets, from where the food article, that is, 'Rasbhari' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 17.03.2004, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) P. C.
Tiwari and Field Assistant (FA) Bhopal Singh under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Dr. Anil Kumar reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Kwality Sweets at WZ-1193, Nangal Rai, New Delhi-46, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Rasbhari from the vendor,
to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 08.04.2004, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained added starch and vegetable oil which were not declared as ingredients.

Upon receipt of report, the In Re vs Ram Singh on 29 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77358429/
1
SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.

After completion of investigation,
sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 06.07.2004 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 06.07.2004.
The accused appeared and stated on 14.07.2004 that he did not want to exercise his right under section 13(2) of PFA Act for sending the sample for analysis to the Central Food Laboratory.
The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence.
4. The prosecution examined PW-1 FI P. C. Tiwari in pre-charge evidence.

On the basis of his testimony, charge was framed against the accused vide order dated 09.03.2009, for commission of offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act,
to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
Upon this, PW-1 was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge evidence.
Additionally, complainant examined FA PW-2 Bhopal Singh and SDM/LHA PW-3 Sh. Anil Aggarwal in post-charge evidence.
5. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 17.03.2004 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Rasbhari,
cutting the same into smallest possible pieces using a clean and dry knife, mixing/homogenizing it,
dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, adding preservative formalin (40 drops each), fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A,
notice Ex. PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, PA Receipt Ex.
PW-1/D and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/E. PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received upon which investigation was carried out.
Letters Ex. PW-1/G and Ex. PW-1/J were written to STO and MCD.
Accused also furnished his reply Ex. PW-1/H. Sanction Ex. PW-1/L
was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/M was then filed in the court.

Copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex.
PW-1/N was sent to the accused vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/O.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sample was not adulterated.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 02.05.2013 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 17.03.2004, yet he claimed that no efforts were made to join public witnesses and that the price of sample was not paid to him.
He stated that the bottled were not clean and dry and claimed that the vegetable oil and starch detected were from pista pieces present in the sample of Rasbhari.
He chose to lead evidence in defence.
7. In defence, the accused examined DW-1 Sh. S. N. Mahendru, a chemical expert.

He deposed that pista contains its own starch and vegetable oil and when fats and oils are extracted in a solvent,
In Re vs Ram Singh on 29 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77358429/
2 inherent oil of pista and inherent fat of rasbhari would come in the solvent.
During cross-examination by the Ld. SPP for complainant, he opined that without identifying the oil or starch, it would be vague to state that there was added oil or added starch in the sample.

8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are missing links in the case.
Ld. Counsel has strongly contended there is no standard prescribed for Rasbhari as a food article and in the absence of prescribed standard, it cannot be said that any Rule has been violated.
It is also submitted that the PA report nowhere shows if the starch and oil detected by it were due to added pista pieces or not.
10. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.

11. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of only section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act, despite the fact that the complaint was filed for violation of section 2(ia)(a)
and (m) of the Act.

Thus, at this stage, the accused is not facing trial for violation of section 2(ia)(m)
of PFA Act.
This is important to note because the ingredients of these offences are different and distinct.

12. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.

On the other hand, section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
13.
In the case at hand, it is an admitted position, as is clear from the report of PA that the food article did not fall under any item of Appendix- B of the PFA Rules.
No standard has been prescribed under the Rules with respect to 'Rasbhari' as a food article as such.
It was thus analysed as a proprietary food.
Proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.

14. In the case at hand, the PA report shows presence of starch in the sample on the basis of iodine test, and presence of vegetable oil as BR reading at 40 deg. of extracted fat was found to be 46.3 which is stated to be exceeding the limits of 40-43.
On this basis, PA concluded that sample contained added starch and vegetable oil which were not declared as ingredients.

15. A perusal of Form-VI, Ex. PW-1/B on the basis of which it is claimed that declaration of ingredients was made by the accused, shows that the accused in his own handwriting has stated that In Re vs Ram Singh on 29 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77358429/
3 the Rasbhari was prepared from Chenna, Sugar and Pista pieces.
It is thus clear that pista pieces had been declared as an ingredient by the accused.
16. It is not the case of the prosecution that use of pista is a prohibited substance or that its use in preparation of Rasbhari is not permitted.
Pista is not an adulterant the use of which would make an offence.
It has been duly proved in the evidence of DW-1, who is a duly recognized and awarded chemical expert in the field of food analysis, that pista has its own inherent fat and starch.
This fact is not even disputed by the prosecution.

Thus, unless the prosecution is able to clearly show that the fat/oil and starch detected by the PA was not a part of pista, it shall not be sufficient to hold that there was presence of added starch or vegetable oil not declared as ingredients.
17. It is not the case of the prosecution that the sample of Rasbhari was having some constituent in quantity not within the prescribed limits.

As already stated, no standards have been prescribed under the Rules with respect to Rasbhari as a food article, and therefore, it cannot be considered that quality or purity of Rasbhari has fallen below the permitted limits of variability.

Had it been so,
the court would have framed charge for violation of section 2(ia)(m) and not section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.
But when no such charge was framed, the court need not even go into that question.

The only fact to be determined is if the case falls in section 2(ia)
(a) of PFA Act under which the accused has been charged.
18.

The basis on which the PA gave report, is that iodine test was positive for presence of starch and BR value of extracted fat was 46.3 which was above the limit of 40-43.
19.
Well, the prosecution has failed to show how this limit of 40-43 has been ascertained to be applicable in case of Rasbhari.
No specific Rule has been shown to exist that shows that this is the maximum permitted value in case of Rasbhari as a food article or any of its constituents.
As already mentioned, Rasbhari is a proprietary food which is not a standardised food article.
20. Similarly, the iodine test only showed presence of starch in the sample analysed.
There is no material to show that this starch is not the natural starch of pista which was already present in the sample, as also observed by the PA upon physical appearance.
No opinion has been given that the starch so detected by iodine test was natural starch or added starch and what was the basis of arriving at such finding.
On the same analogy, there is nothing to show that the oil/fat detected was inherent oil of pista or added oil other than the inherent oil and what was the basis of arriving at the finding given.

21. In such a position, there is substance in the evidence of expert who stated that merely stating that there was added starch or added oil would not serve the purpose, unless such starch or oil is identified.

It is necessary that to get conviction of a person, the prosecution should rule out the possibility of the starch or oil present in a sample to be a part of inherent and natural starch or oil of the pista pieces which were a part of sample analysed.
But there is no such analysis in the report.
It cannot be said with certainty that the starch or oil detected by the PA were not from the pista pieces that had been declared as an ingredient by the accused.

It is quite possible that the tests adopted by In Re vs Ram Singh on 29 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77358429/
4 the PA did not differentiate between the natural or added starch and oil, because there is nothing in report on the basis of which such an opinion has been given by the PA.
22.

Thus, it cannot be concluded that sale of article in question was not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser to his prejudice or was not of nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be, so as to bring it within the purview of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'adulterated'
within the meaning of section 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
23.
Having said so, the accused is entitled to be given benefit of doubt.
He is therefore acquitted of the charges.

However, his bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A. CrPC.
24.
File be consigned to record room.

Announced in the open court this 29th day of March 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
PHC In Re vs Ram Singh on 29 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/77358429/
